daily_reality.typical_workday: OTs work 8-hour days across diverse settings including hospitals, SNFs, outpatient clinics, schools, home health, and mental health facilities. The day begins with reviewing patient charts, checking schedules, and prioritizing caseloads. Core tasks include conducting initial evaluations and functional assessments, developing individualized treatment plans, delivering direct therapy sessions (typically 30-60 minutes each), training patients on adaptive equipment and compensatory strategies, modifying environments for accessibility, and consulting with interdisciplinary teams. Medical OTs see 6-12 patients daily; school-based OTs manage caseloads of 30-60+ students. Documentation consumes 25-40% of the workday, with SOAP notes, evaluation reports, progress notes, and discharge summaries required for every patient encounter. Productivity requirements in many settings demand 80-95% billable time, leaving minimal room for documentation, collaboration, and self-care. Over 133,000 licensed OTs are employed in the US as of 2025, with approximately 9,800 new openings projected each year through 2033.

daily_reality.seasonality: School-based OTs follow the academic calendar with heavy evaluation periods in fall (September-October) and spring (March-April) for IEP meetings. Extended School Year (ESY) services may run during summer for qualifying students. SNF and hospital settings maintain year-round demand with slight increases during winter months (falls, hip fractures, stroke). Home health referrals spike after hospital discharge surges following holiday seasons. Outpatient clinics see increased volume in January (new insurance deductibles reset) and post-summer (return from vacations). Medicare year-end therapy threshold considerations in November-December. Flu season and winter weather increase fall-related injuries driving inpatient rehab volume.

regulatory.licensing: Entry requires either a Master's (MOT/MSOT, 2-3 years) or Doctoral (OTD, 3-3.5 years) degree from an ACOTE-accredited program. Both degrees are accepted as entry-level; AOTA's Representative Assembly placed the 2027 doctoral mandate on hold indefinitely, maintaining dual entry-level pathways. Must complete Level I and Level II fieldwork (minimum 24 weeks of full-time Level II fieldwork). Must pass the NBCOT OTR certification exam. All 50 states and DC require state licensure; core requirements are uniform (accredited degree, fieldwork, NBCOT exam) but states may add specific requirements. Most state licenses renew every 2 years with varying continuing education requirements (typically 12-24 CE hours per renewal cycle). NBCOT certification renewal requires 36 Professional Development Units (PDUs) every 3 years. OTAs (Occupational Therapy Assistants) work under OT supervision with their own NBCOT COTA certification. CMS finalized a change from direct to general supervision of OTAs in private/group practice settings in 2025-2026, aligning with institutional settings.
regulatory.penalties: Practicing without a license: state-specific fines ($1,000-$10,000+), potential misdemeanor/felony charges, and cease-and-desist orders. HIPAA violations: $100 to $50,000 per violation, up to $1.5 million annually per category. AOTA Code of Ethics violations: NBCOT disciplinary action including reprimand, probation, suspension, or revocation of OTR certification. Medicare/Medicaid fraud (upcoding, billing for services not rendered): federal criminal prosecution under False Claims Act, fines up to $50,000 per false claim, treble damages, and exclusion from federal healthcare programs. Failure to maintain continuing education: license suspension or non-renewal. Inadequate supervision of OTAs: disciplinary action by state regulatory board. Productivity-driven ethical violations (double-booking, billing for unseen patients): professional sanctions, license revocation, and potential federal fraud charges. OIG actively audits SNFs for PDPM upcoding and improper therapy billing.

career_psychology.burnout: OT burnout is a significant and growing concern, with research showing 69% of occupational therapists experiencing burnout symptoms. Key drivers include: (1) Unrealistic productivity standards — SNFs commonly require 90-95% billable productivity, outpatient clinics 80-90%, leaving minimal time for documentation, collaboration, and breaks. (2) Documentation burden — many OTs spend 2-3 hours daily on paperwork beyond patient contact hours, often completing notes at home after hours. (3) Value conflicts — pressure to bill maximum units or treat patients who may not need skilled services (particularly in SNFs under PDPM). (4) Declining reimbursement — Medicare conversion factor cuts (2.83% decrease in 2025, proposed 1% RVU cut in 2026) increasing financial pressure on employers who pass it to clinicians. (5) Student loan debt — OTD graduates carrying $80,000-$150,000+ in loans with no significant salary premium over MOT holders. (6) Emotional toll — working with patients experiencing chronic illness, disability, cognitive decline, or end-of-life transitions. OTs with fewer than 10 years of experience report higher burnout. Those working with older adults and in childcare settings report the highest burnout levels, while physical rehabilitation and intellectual disability settings report the lowest. The OTD vs MOT debate adds professional identity stress without clear career benefit.
